title: English trad boom, commercialism and its effect on Australia
summary: British bands imitated George Lewis then commercialised with Barber, Bilk and Ball; Colyer and Mike Daniels stay honest; the trend reaches Australia, even Graham Bell.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well, what about the English trad scene? I mean, as you say, you feel you're very much under the influence of George Lewis. What about the bands over there? Do you feel that they are too imitative? Or that they are going to derive something from this and build it into their own? Are they commercial? Or can you generalise? Or what?

Well, just generally speaking, they came under the George Lewis influence very much some years ago. And quite a few good bands were formed. Some of them were much too imitative. But there were some quite good jazz bands formed. Unfortunately, the jazz scene grew there. And it's become very much commercialised now. There's big money to be made by some bands. Chris Barber showed that first. Followed by Ackerbilk, Kenny Ball. Their jazz content has declined rapidly as they've become popular bands. And unfortunately, that has a big effect on the other bands, the sort of secondary bands, who are also trying to cash in on this. And it's a sorry scene in England now, compared with a few years ago when there were quite a few idealist sort of players still about. But there are still some semi-professional bands who try to play jazz because they like it. Ken Collier is the first one that comes to mind. He still manages to do quite well playing full-time professionally without bowing to all the gimmicks and tricks that the others have to bow to. But other bands. Kid Martin's Ragtime Band, led by Barry Martin, who spent some time here, is a very good band. A chap called Mike Daniels. He has a very nice band. He's had it for ten years. But will not turn professional because he wants to play as he likes. And they've got a fine band. They play Jelly Roll Morton, King Oliver tunes and things like that. But in their own way, they're a good band and a different sort of band. A very happy band. Very impressive. Unfortunately, most of the bands in England are not developing at all in a good way. They're going backwards, getting onto the tradie pops kick.

I've been away from Australia for two years. I'm told that it is. They've had visits from Acker Bilk and from Kenny Bull. And let me say, this Acker Bilk is still playing quite a bit of jazz and much superior stuff to Kenny Bull. But I'm told that there has been a bit of a trad movement that's grown since I left Australia. Of all people, Graham Bell, a sort of pioneer, has got in on it with a band of people who play what I would term slick Dixie. I don't know what effect this is having on the sort of secondary bands there. I hope it's not having too much of an effect on them. But the movement's so much smaller in Australia that there is more chance that the bands will stick to playing their way and not let themselves be ruled by the market too much. Mainly because there's not much of an Acker. So that it's not worth it.
